tip-calculator.intro: Tip Calculator works out the tip, the new total, and each person's share from three numbers: the bill, the tip percentage, and how many people are splitting it. The four preset buttons cover the percentages people actually use in US restaurants, and every figure updates as you type.
how: Enter the bill amount before tip.
Type a tip percentage, or tap one of the 15%, 18%, 20%, or 25% presets.
Set how many people are splitting the bill. One is fine.
Read the tip, the total, and the per-person amount.
method: The tip is the bill multiplied by the percentage divided by 100. The total is the bill plus the tip. The per-person figure is the total divided by the number of people.
Nothing is rounded until it is displayed, so splitting an awkward bill across three or seven people will not quietly lose or invent a cent.

example.setup: The tool opens with a typical dinner for two already filled in.
example.result: Tip $9.70, total $58.20, and $29.10 per person.

uses: Splitting a restaurant bill without doing arithmetic at the table.
Checking whether a suggested tip on a card terminal is what you actually meant to leave.
Working out a per-head figure before you ask everyone for cash.
Budgeting a meal out by working backwards from what you want the total to be.
mistakes: Tipping on the post-tax total. US convention is to tip on the pre-tax subtotal, which is usually a dollar or two less.
Tipping on the pre-discount amount after a coupon. If a voucher covered half the meal, most people still tip on what the food would have cost.
Forgetting that some restaurants add gratuity automatically for large parties, which means an extra tip on top is a second tip.

mortgage-calculator.intro: Mortgage Calculator estimates a full monthly housing payment, not just principal and interest. It folds in property tax, home insurance, and PMI, then shows the amortization schedule so you can see how the split between interest and principal changes over the life of the loan.
how: Enter the home price and your down payment. The dollar and percentage fields stay in sync, so you can drive it from either one.
Set the interest rate and pick a term: 30, 15, 10, or 7 years.
Adjust the property tax rate, annual insurance, and PMI rate if you know your real numbers.
Read the monthly payment breakdown and scroll the amortization schedule.
method: Principal and interest come from the standard amortizing loan formula: M = P x r x (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n - 1), where P is the amount borrowed, r is the monthly interest rate (the annual rate divided by 12), and n is the number of monthly payments.

Property tax and insurance are annual figures divided by 12 and added on. PMI is charged as a percentage of the loan amount per year and only applies while the down payment is under 20%, which is why it disappears from the total the moment you cross that line.

example.setup: Using the values the calculator loads with:
example.result: Borrowing $280,000 gives roughly $1,816 a month in principal and interest, plus about $321 in tax and $100 in insurance, for a total near $2,237. At 20% down there is no PMI.

uses: Checking what a listing price actually costs per month before you tour the house.
Comparing a 30-year and a 15-year term on the same loan to see the real trade between payment size and total interest.
Working out how much extra down payment it takes to clear 20% and drop PMI.
Sanity-checking a lender's quote against an independent calculation.
mistakes: Budgeting on principal and interest alone. Tax and insurance often add several hundred dollars a month and are usually collected in the same payment through escrow.
Assuming PMI is permanent. It normally falls away once you have 20% equity, which happens sooner if home values rise.
Using the advertised rate instead of your quoted rate. Advertised rates usually assume excellent credit and discount points.
notes: The down payment dollar and percent fields update each other, so changing one corrects the other.
PMI is applied only when the down payment is below 20%.
The amortization schedule shows every month, so you can see the exact point where you start paying more principal than interest.

ohms-law.intro: Ohm's Law Calculator solves for voltage, current, resistance, and power. Enter any two of the four and it works out the other two, so you do not have to remember which rearrangement of the formula you need.
how: Type any two known values into the voltage, current, resistance, or power fields.
The remaining two are calculated as soon as there is enough information.
Press Clear All to start a new calculation.
method: Ohm's Law itself is V = I x R: voltage equals current times resistance. Power adds a second relationship, P = V x I.
Combining them gives the two forms people forget: P = I squared x R, and P = V squared / R. Those are what let the calculator finish from any pair of inputs rather than only from voltage and current.

example.setup: A 12 volt supply feeding a 4 ohm load:
example.result: Current is 12 / 4 = 3 A, and power is 12 x 3 = 36 W.

uses: Sizing a series resistor for an LED so it gets the current it is rated for.
Checking whether a resistor's wattage rating is high enough for the power it will actually dissipate.
Working out how much current a load will pull before you choose a power supply or a fuse.
Checking a measured reading against what the circuit should theoretically be doing.
mistakes: Mixing milliamps and amps. A 20 mA LED current is 0.02 A, and entering 20 gives an answer that is off by a thousand.
Confusing a resistor's power rating with the power it dissipates. A quarter-watt resistor asked to dissipate half a watt will run hot and eventually fail.
Applying Ohm's Law directly to non-ohmic parts. Diodes, LEDs, and transistors do not have a fixed resistance, so the law applies to the resistor in the circuit, not to the semiconductor.

base64-encoder.intro: Base64 Encoder converts text into Base64, the encoding used whenever binary or awkward data has to travel through something that only reliably handles plain text. Encoding happens in the page as you type, and the result can be copied in one click.
how: Paste or type the text you want to encode.
The Base64 output appears immediately below.
Use Copy Result to put it on the clipboard, or Clear to start over.
method: Base64 takes three bytes at a time (24 bits) and re-cuts them into four groups of six bits. Each six-bit group becomes one character from a 64-character alphabet of A-Z, a-z, 0-9, plus, and slash.

When the input does not divide evenly into three bytes, the output is padded with one or two equals signs so the length is always a multiple of four. Because four characters carry three bytes, Base64 output is always about 33% larger than the input.

example.setup: Encoding the two-character string Hi:
example.result: SGk= - three characters of data plus one equals sign, because two bytes is not a whole three-byte group.

uses: Embedding a small image or font directly in CSS or HTML as a data URI, removing a network request.
Building an HTTP Basic Authentication header, which is the Base64 of username:password.
Moving configuration or a certificate through a form, a JSON field, or a chat message that would otherwise mangle it.
Inspecting the payload of a JSON Web Token, whose segments are Base64url.
mistakes: Treating Base64 as encryption. It is an encoding, not a cipher. Anyone can decode it instantly, so it hides nothing.
Pasting Base64 into a URL without converting it. Standard Base64 uses plus and slash, which have their own meaning in URLs. The URL-safe variant swaps them for minus and underscore.
Assuming it saves space. It costs roughly a third more than the original, so it is a compatibility tool, not a compression one.

lil-beat-maker.intro: Lil Beat Maker is an eight-track step sequencer that runs in the browser using the Web Audio API. You switch steps on and off in a grid, set the tempo, and it loops. There is no signup, no download, and no sample pack to install.
how: Click cells in the grid to turn steps on. Each row is one drum sound and each column is one step in time.
Choose 16 or 32 steps depending on whether you want a one-bar or two-bar loop.
Drag the BPM slider anywhere from 60 to 200.
Press Play to loop it, Randomize for a starting point, or Load Groove for a preset pattern.
lil-beat-maker.method_title: How the grid maps to time
method: A 16-step grid is one bar of 4/4 counted in sixteenth notes. Columns 1, 5, 9, and 13 are the four downbeats, and everything between them is a subdivision.

Step length follows directly from the tempo. At 120 BPM a quarter note is half a second, so a sixteenth note is 125 milliseconds and the whole 16-step bar loops every 2 seconds. Halve the tempo and every step doubles in length.

example.setup: The classic four-on-the-floor house pattern on a 16-step grid at the default tempo:
example.result: A two-second loop with a kick on every beat, a backbeat on 2 and 4, and eighth-note hats running underneath.

uses: Sketching a drum pattern before you commit to opening a full DAW.
Making a quick loop to practice an instrument over.
Teaching or learning how a beat is actually built, one subdivision at a time.
Testing whether an idea in your head works before you spend an hour producing it.
notes: Everything runs client-side through the Web Audio API, so nothing is uploaded and the page works offline once loaded.
The 32-step mode gives you two bars, which is enough room for a fill or a variation on the second half.
Tempo can be changed while the loop is playing.

hangman.intro: Hangman is the classic word guessing game with category hints, selectable difficulty, full keyboard input, and stats that persist between sessions. Guess the hidden word one letter at a time before you run out of attempts.
how: Pick a category, or leave it on the default for a mixed word list.
Type a letter or click it on the on-screen keyboard.
Correct letters fill into the word. Wrong letters cost you one of your remaining attempts.
Press New Word to start again. Your win and loss record carries over.
method: Open with vowels. E, A, and O appear in the overwhelming majority of English words, and knowing the vowel skeleton narrows the possibilities faster than anything else.

Then go after the common consonants in roughly the order R, S, T, L, N. After that, use the pattern rather than frequency: a word ending in double letters, or a visible -ING or -TION, tells you far more than the next most common letter would.
uses: A short break that does not need an account or an install.
Vocabulary and spelling practice for kids, with categories to keep it on topic.
A no-setup classroom or waiting-room game.
Passing a few minutes without an app store download.
notes: Stats are stored in your browser only, so they survive a refresh but never leave your device.
Both the physical keyboard and the on-screen letters work, so it plays the same on phone and desktop.
Letters already tried are marked, so you cannot waste a guess by repeating one.

guitar-fretboard.intro: Guitar Fretboard shows the note name at every position across all six strings and twelve frets. Pick a root and a scale and the notes in that scale light up, so you can see the shape rather than memorise it position by position.
how: Choose a root note, or leave it on None to see every note name.
Pick a scale or mode to highlight only its notes.
Switch tuning if you are not in standard. Drop D, Open G, DADGAD and E flat standard are all supported.
Read the shapes across the neck and find the same scale in more than one position.
method: Standard tuning is EADGBE from the low string up. Every string is a perfect fourth above the one below it, except the B string, which is a major third above the G. That single exception is why chord and scale shapes shift by one fret once they cross to the top two strings.

Because the guitar is tuned in mostly even intervals, one scale shape works for every root. Move the shape up two frets and you have moved the key up a whole tone, which is why guitarists talk about positions instead of note names.

example.setup: Finding the A minor pentatonic box, the first shape most players learn:
example.result: The highlighted notes cluster at the fifth fret, giving the familiar two-note-per-string box that runs A C D E G.

uses: Learning where a scale actually sits instead of memorising one box shape.
Finding the same notes higher up the neck so you can solo past the fifth fret.
Checking which notes change when you drop to an alternate tuning.
Working out the note under your finger when you are reading a chord chart.
mistakes: Assuming a shape transposes cleanly across the G and B strings. That major third breaks the pattern and shifts everything one fret.
Learning only one pentatonic box. The same five notes exist in five positions and the neck opens up when you connect them.
Forgetting that changing tuning changes every note name on the neck, not just the string you retuned.

bass-fretboard.intro: Bass Fretboard maps note names across four strings and a full twenty-four frets, which is double the range most fretboard charts show. Select a root and a scale and only those notes stay lit.
how: Pick a root note, or leave it on None to see every note.
Choose a scale or mode from major and natural minor through the pentatonics, blues, Dorian and Mixolydian.
Switch tuning to Drop D, E flat standard, or five-string BEADG.
Read the highlighted notes across all twenty-four frets.
bass-fretboard.method_title: How the bass neck is laid out
method: Standard bass tuning is EADG, the same as the lowest four strings of a guitar but an octave down. Every string is a perfect fourth above the one below, with no exception, which is why bass shapes transpose cleanly across the whole neck.
Twelve frets is one octave, so the note at fret 12 on any string is the open string an octave higher. Everything above fret 12 repeats the pattern below it.

example.setup: Locating the E minor pentatonic, the workhorse scale for rock and blues bass lines:
example.result: Notes light up on the open E and around the twelfth fret, showing the same five notes (E G A B D) in two playable positions an octave apart.

uses: Finding a scale in the upper register where most charts stop at fret 12.
Checking what a five-string low B adds before you buy one.
Working out a walking line that stays in key.
Seeing which notes move when you drop to D.
notes: The four-fourths tuning means every shape transposes without the fret shift guitarists deal with.
Twenty-four frets covers two full octaves per string.
Five-string BEADG adds a low B, extending the range down a fourth below the E.

ukulele-fretboard.intro: Ukulele Fretboard shows every note across four strings and twelve frets, with scale highlighting and support for standard, D, and low-G tunings. It is the fastest way to see why the ukulele fingers differently from a guitar.
how: Pick a root note or leave it on None for all note names.
Choose a scale to highlight, from major and minor through pentatonics, blues and the modes.
Switch tuning between standard GCEA, D tuning, and low G.
Read the highlighted notes across the neck.
ukulele-fretboard.method_title: Reentrant tuning, and why it matters
method: Standard ukulele tuning is GCEA, but the G is normally reentrant, meaning it is tuned above the C rather than below it. The strings do not run low to high in pitch order, which is what gives the instrument its bright, chiming sound.
Low G tuning drops that string an octave so the instrument runs in pitch order like a guitar. The fingerings are identical, but scale runs and bass notes sound completely different.

example.setup: Mapping C major, the friendliest key on a ukulele:
example.result: The scale highlights on the open C string and across the first three frets, which is why so many beginner ukulele songs sit in C.

uses: Understanding why a guitar shape does not transfer directly to a ukulele.
Deciding whether low G is worth restringing for.
Finding scale notes for a melody rather than only strumming chords.
Learning the neck past the third fret.
mistakes: Treating the top four guitar strings as identical. Ukulele is tuned a fourth higher, so the same shape gives a different chord name.
Expecting the open G to be the lowest note in standard tuning. In reentrant tuning it is not.

guitar-chords.intro: Guitar Chords is a diagram browser for open and barre chord fingerings. Filter by root and chord type and read the fingering straight off the grid, including which strings to mute and which to play open.
how: Pick a root, or leave it on All Roots to browse everything.
Pick a chord type, or leave it on All Types.
Read the diagram: numbers are fingers, O is an open string, X is a string you do not play.
guitar-chords.method_title: How to read a chord diagram
method: The six vertical lines are the strings, low E on the left through high E on the right. The horizontal lines are frets, with the top line being the nut unless a fret number is marked beside the grid.

A barre chord shows one finger covering several strings at the same fret. Because it uses no open strings, the whole shape can slide up the neck: the same shape two frets higher is the same chord type a whole tone higher.
uses: Looking up a chord you have never played in the middle of a song.
Finding an easier voicing when a barre chord is out of reach.
Learning the four movable shapes that cover most of the neck.
Checking which strings should be muted so the chord sounds clean.
mistakes: Strumming muted strings. An X means that string must not ring, and letting it sound changes the chord.
Pressing behind the fret instead of just behind the fret wire, which is the usual cause of buzzing.
Learning only open chords. Barre shapes are harder at first but give you every key from four shapes.

ukulele-chords.intro: Ukulele Chords is a fingering diagram browser for standard GCEA tuning. Filter by root and chord type and read the shape off the grid, including open strings and any string that should not ring.
how: Choose a root, or All Roots to browse.
Choose a chord type, or All Types.
Read the four-string diagram: numbers are fingers, O is open, X is muted.
method: Four strings instead of six means most chords need only one, two or three fingers. C major is a single finger on the third fret of the A string.

Because the ukulele has only four strings, chords often leave out the fifth of the chord. That is why a ukulele chord can sound thinner than the same chord on guitar, and why the voicings are not simply guitar shapes moved across.
uses: Learning a song quickly, since most ukulele songs use four or five chords.
Finding a simpler voicing for a chord that looks awkward.
Checking a chord you know on guitar to see what it becomes on ukulele.
Building a first chord vocabulary: C, F, G and A minor cover a huge amount of repertoire.
notes: All diagrams assume standard GCEA tuning.
Shapes without open strings can be moved up the neck to change key.

piano-chords.intro: Piano Chords shows any chord on an interactive keyboard and plays it back, so you can see the shape and hear whether you have the right voicing. Pick a root, a chord type and an octave.
how: Select a root note.
Select a chord type.
Choose an octave: 3 for low, 4 for middle C, 5 for high.
Read the highlighted keys and listen to the chord.
method: Every chord here is built by counting semitones up from the root. A major triad is the root, four semitones, then three more (0, 4, 7). A minor triad flips that to 0, 3, 7. Diminished is 0, 3, 6 and augmented is 0, 4, 8.
Seventh chords add a fourth note. A dominant seventh is 0, 4, 7, 10. A major seventh raises that top note to 11, which is the single semitone that separates a bluesy sound from a dreamy one.

example.setup: Building C major in the middle of the keyboard:
example.result: C, E and G light up. Counting from C: E is four semitones up, G is three above E.

uses: Checking a chord symbol you have never played before.
Hearing the difference between major seventh and dominant seventh rather than reading about it.
Teaching chord construction visually.
Finding a voicing in a comfortable octave for singing.
mistakes: Confusing a major seventh with a dominant seventh. Cmaj7 and C7 differ by one semitone and sound nothing alike.
Always playing chords in root position. Inversions move more smoothly between chords.

chord-finder.intro: Chord Finder works backwards. Click the notes you are holding down on the piano keyboard and it tells you what chord that is, including every alternative name and which inversion you are playing.
how: Click the notes on the keyboard, in any order.
Read the matching chord names.
Check the inversion label to see whether the lowest note is the root.
chord-finder.method_title: Why one set of notes has several names
method: A chord is identified by the intervals between its notes, not by the order you played them. The same three notes can be described from different roots, which is why C, E and G is C major but E, G and C is C major in first inversion.

Some note sets are genuinely ambiguous. A diminished seventh chord stacks four notes each three semitones apart, so it has four equally valid names depending on which note you call the root. The tool lists all matches rather than guessing.
uses: Naming a chord you found by ear on the keyboard.
Working out what a chord in sheet music actually is.
Checking whether a voicing you like is a standard chord or something more unusual.
Understanding inversions by hearing them named as you move the bass note.
mistakes: Assuming there is one right answer. Ambiguous chords legitimately have several names, and context decides which is correct.
Ignoring the bass note. The lowest note determines the inversion and often changes how the chord functions.

chords-in-keys.intro: Chords in Keys lists all seven diatonic chords for any key and mode, with Roman numerals. It answers the question every songwriter asks early: which chords are allowed to go together.
how: Pick a root note.
Pick a mode: major, natural minor, or one of Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian and Locrian.
Read the seven chords with their Roman numerals and qualities.
chords-in-keys.method_title: Where the seven chords come from
method: Take the seven notes of the scale, then build a chord on each one by stacking every other note. What quality you get is decided by the scale itself, not by choice.

In any major key the pattern is fixed: I major, ii minor, iii minor, IV major, V major, vi minor, and vii diminished. Natural minor uses the same seven chords starting from the sixth degree, giving i, ii diminished, III, iv, v, VI, VII.

example.setup: The diatonic chords of C major:
example.result: C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am and B diminished. No sharps or flats, which is why C major is where most people start.

uses: Writing a progression that stays in key.
Working out the key of a song from the chords it uses.
Finding a substitute chord that still fits.
Understanding why the vi chord is minor in every major key.
mistakes: Expecting the V chord to be minor in a minor key. Most minor-key songs raise the seventh degree to make V major, which is what creates the pull back to the tonic.
Treating the diminished vii as unusable. It works well as a passing chord even though it rarely gets its own bar.

common-chord-progressions.intro: Common Chord Progressions is a reference library of the progressions that actually get used, filtered by genre and transposed into any key. Each one is shown as Roman numerals and as real chord names.
how: Pick a key and a mode.
Filter by genre: pop, rock, blues, jazz, folk or classical.
Read each progression as Roman numerals and as chords in your chosen key.
common-chord-progressions.method_title: Why Roman numerals instead of chord names
method: Roman numerals describe a progression by scale degree rather than by key, so I-V-vi-IV is the same progression whether you play it in C or in E. Uppercase means major, lowercase means minor.
That is what makes progressions portable. Once you know I-V-vi-IV, you can play it in any of the twelve keys by reading off the diatonic chords for that key.

example.setup: The four-chord progression behind a large share of pop music, in C:
example.result: C, G, Am, F. The same four numerals in G give G, D, Em, C.

uses: Starting a song when a blank page is the problem.
Recognising why two songs sound alike.
Finding a genre-appropriate progression to practise over.
Transposing a progression into a key that suits a singer.
notes: Every progression is shown in both Roman numerals and real chord names for the selected key.
Major and minor mode both have their own progression sets.

chord-transposer.intro: Chord Transposer moves a whole chord sheet from one key to another. Paste the sheet, choose the original and target keys, and every chord symbol shifts while your lyrics and layout stay exactly where they were.
how: Paste a chord sheet, or press Load example to see the format.
Set the original key and the target key.
Choose whether the output prefers sharps or flats.
Press Copy to take the transposed sheet.
method: Transposing means moving every chord by the same number of semitones. Going from C to D is up two semitones, so every chord in the sheet moves up two: C becomes D, Am becomes Bm, F becomes G.

The sharps or flats choice matters because the same pitch has two names. B flat and A sharp are the same note, but keys are conventionally written one way or the other, and mixing them makes a sheet hard to read.

example.setup: Moving a song down to suit a lower voice:
example.result: E, B, C sharp minor, A. Every chord moved down three semitones and the lyrics are untouched.

uses: Dropping a song into a range a singer can actually reach.
Moving a piece into a key with easier guitar shapes.
Matching a chord sheet to a recording in a different key.
Preparing the same song in two keys for different players.
mistakes: Transposing by ear halfway and losing track. Every chord has to move by the same interval or the song stops working.
Ignoring the sharps and flats preference and ending up with a sheet mixing both, which is technically correct and genuinely hard to read.

chord-formulas.intro: Chord Formulas is a reference chart for how chords are built, from basic triads through seventh chords and extensions. Each entry gives the interval formula so you can construct the chord from any root.
method: A formula lists scale degrees relative to the major scale of the root. 1-3-5 is a major triad. Flattening the third gives 1-b3-5, a minor triad. Flattening the fifth as well gives 1-b3-b5, diminished.

Seventh chords add a fourth degree. 1-3-5-7 is a major seventh, 1-3-5-b7 is a dominant seventh, and 1-b3-5-b7 is a minor seventh. Extensions past the seventh (9, 11, 13) continue stacking thirds beyond the octave.

example.setup: Building an A dominant seventh from the formula:
given: A B C# D E F# G#
example.result: A, C sharp, E, G. The flattened seventh is what makes it sound like blues rather than a resolved major seventh.

uses: Constructing a chord on any instrument when you know the root.
Understanding what a chord symbol is actually asking for.
Working out which note to alter when a chart says something like 7#9.
Learning why some chords sound tense and others resolved.
mistakes: Reading the numbers as scale steps of the key rather than of the chord's own root. Formulas are always relative to the root's major scale.
Assuming a 9 chord contains a 7. By convention it does, and a chord with a 9 but no 7 is written add9.

key-signatures.intro: Key Signatures is a complete reference for all thirty major and minor key signatures, showing the sharps or flats in each and how every major key pairs with its relative minor.
how: Filter by major, minor, sharps, flats, or no accidentals.
Read the accidentals in each key signature and the relative key it shares them with.
key-signatures.method_title: The order of sharps and flats
method: Sharps always appear in the same order: F, C, G, D, A, E, B. Flats appear in exactly the reverse order: B, E, A, D, G, C, F. That order never changes, so a signature with three sharps is always F sharp, C sharp and G sharp.

To name a sharp key, take the last sharp and go up one semitone. Three sharps ends on G sharp, so the key is A major. For flat keys, the second-to-last flat is the key name, which is why four flats (B, E, A, D) is A flat major.

example.setup: Identifying a key signature with two sharps:
example.result: D major, or its relative minor B minor. Both share the same two sharps.

uses: Naming a key from the signature at the start of a piece.
Finding the relative minor when a piece sounds minor but has a major signature.
Checking which notes are sharpened or flattened before you sight-read.
Learning the circle of fifths in a way that sticks.
mistakes: Reading a signature as major without listening. A major key and its relative minor share an identical signature, and only the music tells you which it is.
Forgetting that a key signature applies to every octave, not just the line or space where the symbol sits.

metronome.intro: Metronome gives you a click, a visual beat, and a tempo slider from 20 to 280 BPM. There is a tap tempo button for matching a tempo you already have in your head, and preset buttons for the standard Italian tempo markings.
how: Drag the slider to a tempo, or tap the Tap button in time to set it by feel.
Use a preset if you are working from a score marking: Largo 52, Adagio 66, Andante 84, Moderato 108, Allegro 132, Presto 176.
Press Start. Watch the visual beat as well as listening, which helps in a noisy room.
method: Beats per minute counts quarter notes in most time signatures, so 120 BPM means one beat every 500 milliseconds. Halving the tempo doubles the gap between clicks.

Tap tempo works by measuring the time between your taps and averaging it. Four or five taps gives a far steadier reading than two, because a single early or late tap has less influence on the average.

example.setup: Practising a passage marked Andante:
example.result: A click roughly every three quarters of a second, which is the walking pace Andante literally describes.

uses: Practising a difficult passage slowly and raising the tempo in small steps.
Keeping a recording take in time without printing a click into the mix.
Checking whether you are rushing, which almost everyone does under the pressure of a hard bar.
Setting a tempo from a score marking rather than guessing.
mistakes: Practising fast before it is clean. Speed built on top of mistakes just makes the mistakes faster.
Raising the tempo in large jumps. Five BPM at a time holds up far better than twenty.
Only listening. Watching the visual beat catches drift that your ear will forgive.

bpm-counter.intro: BPM Counter measures tempo by tapping. Hit the button or any key in time with the music and it calculates beats per minute live, refining the figure with every tap.
how: Tap the button or press any key in time with the beat.
Keep tapping. The reading gets steadier as more taps are averaged.
Press Reset to start a new measurement.
method: The tool records the time between consecutive taps and averages those intervals. Because there are 60,000 milliseconds in a minute, BPM is simply 60,000 divided by the average interval.
Averaging is why the number settles down as you go. Two taps give one interval and inherit all of its error. Eight taps give seven intervals, and a single sloppy tap barely moves the result.

example.setup: Tapping along to a track at a steady half-second pulse:
example.result: 120 BPM, the most common tempo in pop and house music.

uses: Finding the tempo of a song so you can practise or produce at the same speed.
Matching two tracks before beatmatching them.
Working out the tempo of a piece with no marking on the score.
Checking whether a live performance is drifting from the intended tempo.
mistakes: Tapping on every other beat, which halves the reading. Tap the pulse you would clap.
Stopping after two taps. Give it at least four before trusting the number.
Tapping to the snare in a fast track when the actual beat is twice as quick, or the reverse.

chromatic-scale.intro: Chromatic Scale is an interactive reference for all twelve pitches in Western music. Click any note to hear it and see its enharmonic equivalent, in your choice of three octaves.
how: Choose an octave: 3 for low, 4 for middle, 5 for high.
Click any of the twelve notes to hear it.
Read the enharmonic equivalent shown alongside each altered note.
chromatic-scale.method_title: Twelve notes, more than twelve names
method: Western music divides the octave into twelve equal semitones. Play all twelve in order and you have the chromatic scale, which is the raw material every other scale is carved out of.

Five of those twelve have two names each. C sharp and D flat are the same key on a piano but are written differently depending on the key you are in. Sharps are used when a note is rising, flats when it is falling, which is why the same pitch changes name between contexts.

example.setup: The chromatic scale starting on C:
given: C, C#, D, D#, E, F, F#, G, G#, A, A#, B
example.result: Twelve pitches, seven letter names, and five notes that carry two spellings each.

uses: Hearing the difference between a semitone and a whole tone.
Checking which enharmonic spelling belongs in a given key.
Learning where the semitones fall between E and F, and between B and C, where there is no black key.
Ear training on individual pitches.
mistakes: Assuming every letter has a sharp. E sharp is F and B sharp is C, because those pairs are already only a semitone apart.
Treating enharmonics as interchangeable in notation. They sound identical but only one spelling is correct in a given key.

diatonic-scale.intro: Diatonic Scale is a full reference for any major key. Pick a key and it shows the seven scale notes, the triads built on each degree, the seventh chords, and the Roman numeral for every one.
how: Select a key.
Read the seven scale notes in order.
Read the triad and seventh chord built on each degree, with its Roman numeral.
diatonic-scale.method_title: The pattern that defines a major scale
method: Every major scale follows the same step pattern: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. That fixed pattern is what makes every major scale sound like a major scale regardless of which note you start on.

The chord qualities follow automatically from that pattern and never change: I major, ii minor, iii minor, IV major, V major, vi minor, vii diminished. You do not choose them, the scale hands them to you.

example.setup: Building G major from the step pattern:
given: W W H W W W H
G A B C D E F#
example.result: One sharp (F sharp), which is exactly what the key signature for G major shows.

uses: Seeing every chord available in a key at once.
Understanding why a particular note has to be sharpened or flattened.
Finding the seventh chords when a triad sounds too plain.
Learning Roman numeral analysis on real keys.
mistakes: Counting the semitone steps wrong between the third and fourth degrees. That half step is what separates major from every other mode.
Forgetting that the eighth note is the first one again, an octave up, so a scale has seven distinct notes and not eight.

pentatonic-scale.intro: Pentatonic Scale Explorer shows major and minor pentatonic scales for any root on a piano keyboard, and plays them back. Five notes per octave instead of seven, which is why these scales are so forgiving to improvise with.
how: Pick a root note.
Choose Major Pentatonic or Minor Pentatonic.
Press Play to hear the scale, and read the highlighted keys.
pentatonic-scale.method_title: What gets left out, and why it matters
method: A major pentatonic takes the major scale and removes the fourth and seventh degrees, leaving 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6. Those two removed notes are the ones that create the strongest dissonance against the tonic chord, which is why what remains sounds consonant against almost anything.

A minor pentatonic is 1, flat 3, 4, 5 and flat 7. It is the same five pitches as the major pentatonic a minor third above it, which is why A minor pentatonic and C major pentatonic contain identical notes and simply resolve to different homes.

example.setup: Comparing the two pentatonic types on the same five pitches:
example.result: Identical notes, different root. The tonal centre, not the note set, is what makes one sound bright and the other sound bluesy.

uses: Improvising over a chord progression without hitting a wrong note.
Writing a melody that stays singable.
Learning your first soloing vocabulary on guitar or piano.
Understanding why so much folk and blues music worldwide uses five notes.
mistakes: Playing only the five notes and never leaving them. The removed notes are exactly what create tension, so avoiding them forever makes solos bland.
Assuming major and minor pentatonic are unrelated. They are the same set viewed from different roots.

scale-formulas.intro: Scale Formulas is a reference chart of whole and half step patterns for major, minor, the seven modes, pentatonics, blues and more. Every scale is given as its interval pattern so you can build it from any root.
method: A scale formula is a sequence of steps: W for a whole tone (two semitones) and H for a half tone (one semitone). Apply the pattern from any starting note and you get that scale in that key.

The modes are all the same seven notes as a major scale started from a different degree. Dorian is the major pattern started from the second degree, Mixolydian from the fifth. That is why they share a key signature but sound completely different, since the tonal centre has moved.

example.setup: Applying the Dorian pattern from D:
given: W H W W W H W
D E F G A B C
example.result: The white keys from D to D. Same notes as C major, but D is home, which gives Dorian its minor sound with a raised sixth.

uses: Building any scale from any root without memorising all twelve keys.
Understanding what actually separates one mode from another.
Finding the one altered note that changes a scale's character.
Transferring a scale between instruments.
mistakes: Thinking the modes are difficult because they have Greek names. Each is just a major scale started somewhere else.
Counting the last step wrong. Every seven-note scale formula has seven steps that add up to twelve semitones and land back on the octave.

scale-finder.intro: Scale Finder builds any scale from a root note and a scale type, showing every note, the intervals between them, and the scale degrees on a mini keyboard.
how: Pick a root note.
Pick a scale type.
Read the notes, intervals and degree numbers, and see the shape on the keyboard.
method: The notes tell you what to play. The intervals tell you the distance between consecutive notes. The degrees tell you each note's function relative to the root, which is the part that transfers to other keys.
Degrees are what let you talk about music portably. The fifth degree pulls toward the root in every key, so once you hear that relationship you can use it anywhere.
uses: Working out the notes of an unfamiliar scale.
Comparing two scales to see which notes actually differ.
Finding a scale that fits a chord you are improvising over.
Checking a scale before writing it into a part.
mistakes: Learning notes without degrees. Note names change with every key, degrees never do.
Assuming a scale name means one fixed thing. Minor alone can mean natural, harmonic or melodic, and they differ in the sixth and seventh degrees.

music-intervals.intro: Music Intervals is a full reference for interval names, abbreviations, semitone counts and audible examples, covering everything from a unison to an octave and beyond into compound intervals.
method: An interval is measured in semitones but named by letter distance, which is why the two do not always agree. C to E spans four semitones and three letter names (C, D, E), so it is a major third rather than a fourth.

The twelve intervals inside an octave are: unison 0, minor second 1, major second 2, minor third 3, major third 4, perfect fourth 5, tritone 6, perfect fifth 7, minor sixth 8, major sixth 9, minor seventh 10, major seventh 11, octave 12.

example.setup: Identifying the interval from C to G:
given: C D E F G, so five
example.result: A perfect fifth. It is the interval at the root of almost every chord and the reason the circle of fifths works.

uses: Naming an interval you hear or see written.
Building chords, since every chord is a stack of specific intervals.
Ear training by associating each interval with a song that opens on it.
Understanding why some pairs of notes sound stable and others tense.
mistakes: Counting semitones and calling it the interval name. A diminished fourth and a major third are both four semitones but are spelled and used differently.
Forgetting the tritone is neither major nor minor. At exactly six semitones it sits halfway and belongs to neither family.

music-theory-cheat-sheet.intro: Music Theory Cheat Sheet collects the reference material you keep looking up: intervals, scale formulas, chord construction, the circle of fifths, key signatures and common progressions, all on one page.
method: Almost all of Western theory follows from two ideas. First, the octave is divided into twelve equal semitones. Second, a major scale picks seven of them using the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.

Everything else is built on that. Chords are alternate notes from a scale stacked up. Keys are scales given a home note. The circle of fifths is what you get when you order the twelve keys by how many notes they share, which is why keys next to each other on it sound related.
uses: Checking a formula mid-practice without hunting through a textbook.
Revising before a theory exam or an audition.
Settling an argument about what a chord symbol means.
Teaching, where having every reference on one page saves time.
notes: Covers intervals, scales and modes, chord construction, key signatures, the circle of fifths and common progressions.
Written as reference material rather than a course, so it assumes you want the answer rather than the lesson.

note-identification.intro: Note Identification is a sight-reading trainer. A note appears on a treble or bass staff and you name it, with three difficulty levels and an option to hear the pitch as well as see it.
how: Choose treble or bass clef.
Pick a range: Easy for lines only, Medium for lines and spaces, Hard to include ledger lines.
Name the note shown, and use Hear note to connect the symbol to the sound.
note-identification.method_title: The mnemonics, and what to do after them
method: Treble clef lines from the bottom are E, G, B, D, F, and the spaces spell FACE. Bass clef lines are G, B, D, F, A and the spaces are A, C, E, G.

Mnemonics get you started but they are slow, because reciting a sentence takes longer than reading a word. Fluent readers recognise landmark notes on sight (the G that the treble clef curls around, the F between the bass clef dots) and count a step or two from there.
uses: Building sight-reading speed with short, frequent practice.
Learning the second clef when you already read one fluently.
Getting comfortable with ledger lines, which is where most readers stall.
Connecting written pitch to actual sound through the playback option.
mistakes: Practising only treble clef. The bass clef is not harder, it is just less practised.
Skipping ledger lines because they are uncomfortable. That discomfort is the reason to practise them.
Long rare sessions instead of short daily ones. Sight-reading responds to frequency more than duration.

piano-notes-on-staff.intro: Piano Notes on Staff connects the keyboard to written notation. Click any piano key and the matching note appears on the treble and bass staff, with its name and octave number.
how: Click any key on the piano.
Watch where the note lands on the grand staff.
Read the note name and octave number shown alongside.
piano-notes-on-staff.method_title: How the grand staff maps to the keyboard
method: Piano music uses two staves at once. The treble staff normally carries the right hand and the bass staff the left, and together they cover the keyboard's range without needing endless ledger lines.

Middle C sits exactly between them, on one ledger line below the treble staff or one ledger line above the bass staff. It is the same key on the piano written two ways, which is the single fact that makes the grand staff click for most beginners.
uses: Learning to read notation by connecting it to a key you can see.
Working out where a written note actually is on the keyboard.
Understanding middle C and why it appears on both staves.
Checking octave numbering, where C4 is middle C.
mistakes: Assuming the treble staff always means the right hand. Music crosses staves freely when the writing calls for it.
Reading ledger lines by counting from the staff every time instead of learning the common ones by sight.

clef-reference.intro: Clef Reference maps every note position on both treble and bass staves, including the ledger lines above and below where most readers lose their footing.
clef-reference.method_title: Why there are two clefs at all
method: A staff has only five lines, which covers about an octave and a half before you need ledger lines. Two clefs positioned at different pitches let a piano's full range be written without stacking ledger lines that nobody can read at speed.

The clef symbol itself is a pointer. The treble clef curls around the line that is G above middle C. The bass clef's two dots sit either side of the line that is F below middle C. Every other note is counted from there.

example.setup: Locating the same pitch on both staves:
given: one ledger line below the staff
one ledger line above the staff
example.result: Both are middle C, the same key on the piano, written from the perspective of each clef.

uses: Looking up a note position without working it out from a mnemonic.
Learning ledger lines systematically instead of by trial and error.
Switching between clefs when you play an instrument that uses both.
Checking a note when transcribing.
notes: Covers both clefs including ledger lines above and below each staff.
Shows how the two staves overlap around middle C.

virtual-piano.intro: Virtual Piano is a playable two-octave keyboard that runs entirely in the browser using the Web Audio API. Play with the mouse or your computer keyboard, and shape the sound with waveform, sustain and volume controls.
how: Click the keys, or use your computer keyboard to play.
Pick a waveform: sine, triangle, square or sawtooth.
Adjust sustain from 0.3 to 3 seconds and set the volume.
virtual-piano.method_title: What the waveform control actually changes
method: Each waveform has a different harmonic content, which is what your ear hears as tone colour. A sine wave is a single pure frequency with no harmonics at all, so it sounds soft and flute-like. A triangle adds quiet odd harmonics and sounds slightly hollow.

A square wave has strong odd harmonics and sounds buzzy and retro. A sawtooth contains every harmonic and is the brightest and thickest of the four, which is why it is the usual starting point for synth string and brass sounds.
uses: Trying out a chord or melody when there is no instrument nearby.
Hearing the difference between waveforms, which is the first lesson in synthesis.
Checking a pitch or interval while working on something else.
Teaching keyboard layout without needing hardware.
notes: Sound is generated live by the Web Audio API rather than played from samples, so nothing is downloaded.
Longer sustain makes chords ring into each other, which is useful for hearing how voicings blend.

xylophone.intro: Xylophone is a playable two-octave instrument with colour-coded bars. Click a bar or use your keyboard, and choose the waveform and volume that suit the sound you want.
how: Click the bars, or play with your computer keyboard.
Choose a waveform: triangle, sine or square.
Set the volume between 0.1 and 0.6.
xylophone.method_title: Why a xylophone sounds the way it does
method: A real xylophone is a struck idiophone with wooden bars. The sound decays almost immediately, which is what makes it read as percussive rather than sustained, and it is why xylophone parts use repeated notes where a string instrument would hold one.
The triangle waveform is the default here because its quiet odd harmonics come closest to a struck wooden bar. A sine is purer and softer, a square is harder and more electronic.
uses: Introducing children to pitch and melody with immediate visual feedback.
Picking out a simple tune without an instrument.
Hearing how the same melody changes with different tone colours.
Classroom use where real instruments are not available.
notes: Two full octaves of colour-coded bars.
Keyboard input works as well as clicking, so you can play faster passages.

drum-patterns.intro: Drum Patterns is a reference library and sequencer in one. Browse the patterns that define rock, funk, jazz, reggae, hip-hop and Latin styles, then play them back at any tempo from 50 to 200 BPM.
how: Filter by genre, or view all patterns.
Select a pattern to see the grid and hear it.
Drag the BPM slider to hear it at the tempo you are working at.
drum-patterns.method_title: The backbeat, and how genres differ from it
method: The standard rock beat puts the kick on beats 1 and 3 and the snare on 2 and 4, with eighth notes on the hi-hat. That snare on 2 and 4 is the backbeat, and it is the backbone of most popular music.

Genres are largely defined by how they depart from it. Funk keeps the backbeat but crowds the kick into sixteenth-note syncopations. Reggae drops or displaces beat 1 entirely and emphasises 3. Jazz moves the timekeeping to the ride cymbal in a swung triplet feel and uses the snare for comments rather than the pulse.

example.setup: The basic rock beat on a 16-step grid:
example.result: The pattern underneath a very large share of rock and pop recordings.

uses: Learning what actually distinguishes one genre's groove from another.
Finding a pattern to practise an instrument over.
Programming drums when you do not play them.
Hearing a pattern slowly before trying to play it up to tempo.
notes: Patterns cover rock, funk, jazz, reggae, hip-hop and Latin.
Tempo is adjustable while a pattern plays.

guitar-tuning-chart.intro: Guitar Tuning Chart lists the string-by-string notes for standard and alternate tunings, grouped into standard, drop, open and modal categories.
how: Filter by category, or view all tunings.
Read the six string notes from low to high for each tuning.
guitar-tuning-chart.method_title: What each family of tuning is for
method: Standard is EADGBE from the lowest string up. Drop tunings lower the sixth string only, so Drop D is DADGBE, which lets a power chord be played with one finger across the bottom three strings.

Open tunings retune the strings so the open guitar sounds a full chord. Open G is DGDGBD, which is why slide players use it: barring any single fret gives a complete major chord. Modal tunings like DADGAD avoid the third entirely, leaving a chord that is neither major nor minor and sits well under folk and Celtic playing.

example.setup: Comparing standard with Drop D:
given: E A D G B E
D A D G B E
sixth string down one whole tone
example.result: One string moves. The low D lets you play a D5 power chord by barring the bottom three strings at one fret.

uses: Retuning correctly for a song written in an alternate tuning.
Choosing a tuning that suits slide or fingerstyle playing.
Understanding why a familiar chord shape produces a different chord after retuning.
Working out how far each string has to move before you start.
mistakes: Tuning a string up too far. Raising pitch increases tension and is the usual way strings break.
Expecting standard chord shapes to work in an open tuning. The whole point is that they do not.

rhythm-challenge.intro: Rhythm Challenge is an ear and timing trainer. It shows a rhythm pattern, plays it, and asks you to tap it back, then scores your accuracy in milliseconds against the actual beat positions.
how: Pick a difficulty: quarter notes only, quarter plus eighth, or eighth plus sixteenth.
Choose a tempo from 60 to 120 BPM.
Listen to the pattern, use Replay if you need it, then tap it back.
Read your timing accuracy and press New Pattern to continue.
method: Your taps are compared to where each note should fall, and the difference is reported in milliseconds. Trained musicians typically land within 20 to 30 ms of the beat, and most listeners cannot hear an error smaller than about 20 ms at all.

Tempo changes how forgiving the exercise is. At 60 BPM a quarter note lasts a full second and there is room to correct. At 120 BPM a sixteenth note lasts 125 ms, so the same absolute error is a much larger fraction of the note.

example.setup: Working out how tight the timing window is at each end of the tempo range:
example.result: A 30 ms error is 3% of a quarter note at 60 BPM but nearly a quarter of a sixteenth note at 120.

uses: Training timing accuracy with objective feedback instead of guesswork.
Practising subdivision, which is where most rhythmic errors come from.
Warming up before a rehearsal or a take.
Finding out whether you rush or drag, since the error has a direction.
mistakes: Starting at the hardest difficulty. Sixteenth-note patterns punish an unsteady internal pulse rather than teaching one.
Tapping along with the playback instead of reproducing the pattern from memory. Copying in real time trains a different skill.

loan-calculator.intro: Loan Calculator works out the monthly payment, the total interest, and a full amortization schedule for any fixed-rate loan. It also handles extra monthly payments, and shows how much interest and time they actually save. The schedule exports to CSV.
how: Enter the loan amount, annual interest rate, and term in years.
Add an extra monthly payment if you plan to overpay. Leave it at zero if not.
Read the monthly payment, total interest and total cost.
Scroll the amortization schedule, or use Export CSV to open it in a spreadsheet.
method: The monthly payment comes from M = P x r x (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n - 1), where P is the amount borrowed, r is the monthly rate (annual rate divided by 12) and n is the total number of payments.

Every payment is split between interest and principal. Interest is charged on the balance that is still outstanding, so early payments are mostly interest and later ones are mostly principal. That is why an extra payment made in year one saves far more than the same payment made in year four.

example.setup: Using the values the calculator loads with:
example.result: About $489 a month, roughly $29,345 paid in total, of which about $4,345 is interest.

uses: Comparing car loan offers where the rate and term both differ.
Seeing what an extra $50 a month actually saves over the life of a loan.
Checking a lender's quoted payment against an independent calculation.
Deciding between a shorter term with higher payments and a longer one with more total interest.
mistakes: Comparing loans on monthly payment alone. A longer term always looks cheaper monthly and usually costs far more overall.
Confusing the interest rate with the APR. APR folds in fees, so it is the fairer number for comparing offers.
Assuming overpayments always reduce the term. Some lenders apply them to the next payment instead of the principal unless you specify.

transfer-time-estimator.intro: Transfer Time Estimator tells you how long a file will take to move at a given connection speed, and shows the same file at a range of common speeds so you can see what upgrading would actually buy you.
how: Enter the file size and pick its unit: KB, MB, GB or TB.
Enter the transfer speed and pick its unit. Both bit rates (Kbps, Mbps, Gbps) and byte rates (KB/s, MB/s, GB/s) are supported.
Read the estimated time, and the comparison table of the same file at common speeds.
transfer-time-estimator.method_title: Bits, bytes, and the factor of eight
method: The single biggest source of confusion is that connection speeds are quoted in bits per second while file sizes are given in bytes. There are eight bits in a byte, so a 100 Mbps connection moves at most about 12.5 MB per second.

Real transfers never hit the theoretical figure. Protocol overhead, latency, disk speed and contention with other traffic typically cost 10 to 20 percent, so treat the result as a floor rather than a promise.

example.setup: The default case, a 1 GB file on a 100 Mbps connection:
example.result: About 80 seconds at the theoretical maximum. Expect closer to 90 to 100 seconds in practice.

uses: Deciding whether to wait for an upload or start it and walk away.
Checking whether a faster internet plan would meaningfully change your workflow.
Estimating a backup or sync window before you start one.
Explaining to someone why their 100 Mbps connection does not download a 1 GB file in ten seconds.
mistakes: Reading Mbps as megabytes per second. It is megabits, and the difference is a factor of eight.
Forgetting that upload speed is usually much slower than download on home connections.
Assuming the bottleneck is the network. On fast connections the hard drive or the far-end server is often the limit.

meeting-agenda-builder.intro: Meeting Agenda Builder turns a list of topics into a timed agenda with owners and a running total, then copies it out as clean plain text or Markdown ready to paste into a calendar invite or a document.
how: Fill in the meeting title, the date or context, and the goal.
Add agenda items with a duration and an owner for each.
Watch the total length update so you can see when you have overbooked the slot.
Copy as plain text or Markdown, whichever your destination handles better.
meeting-agenda-builder.method_title: Why timing each item changes the meeting
method: An untimed agenda is a wish list. Assigning minutes to each item forces the trade-off out into the open before the meeting rather than in the last five minutes of it, when the final item silently gets dropped.
Naming an owner per item does the same for responsibility. An item with no owner has no one preparing for it, which is the usual reason a topic gets deferred to the next meeting.

example.setup: A 30-minute team sync, built from the example the tool loads:
given: each with minutes and an owner
example.result: A running total that tells you immediately whether the agenda fits the half hour or needs cutting.

uses: Preparing an agenda to paste into a calendar invite before sending it.
Keeping a recurring meeting from expanding to fill its slot.
Making it obvious when a 30-minute meeting has 45 minutes of content.
Producing a Markdown agenda for a wiki or a pull request description.
mistakes: Scheduling every minute. Leave slack, because discussion never lands exactly on the estimate.
Writing a goal that is really a topic. Align on priorities is a goal; Q3 planning is a subject heading.
Putting the most important item last, where it is the one that gets cut.

unit-price-calculator.intro: Unit Price Calculator compares products by cost per unit so you can tell which package is actually cheaper. Add as many products as you want and set the unit label to whatever you are measuring in.
how: Set the unit label to match what you are comparing: oz, kg, sheets, litres, whatever fits.
Add each product with its price and its size.
Read the cost per unit for each and compare directly.
unit-price-calculator.method_title: Why bigger is not always cheaper
method: Unit price is simply the total price divided by the quantity. It is the only number that lets you compare a 12 ounce jar against an 18 ounce jar at different prices.

Retailers know shoppers assume the large size is better value, and it often is not. Comparing per unit is the only reliable check, and shelf labels frequently use inconsistent units between competing brands to make it harder.
uses: Grocery shopping where the same product comes in three sizes.
Comparing bulk purchases against buying as you go.
Checking whether a multi-buy offer is genuinely cheaper per item.
Comparing two brands that package in different quantities.
mistakes: Comparing across different units without converting. A price per litre and a price per fluid ounce cannot be compared directly.
Ignoring waste. The cheapest unit price is not a saving if you throw half of it away.
Trusting the shelf unit price without checking. They are frequently wrong or use a different unit than the product beside them.

calorie-deficit.intro: Calorie Deficit Calculator works backwards from a goal. Enter your current weight, your target weight, and the date you want to reach it, and it tells you the daily calorie deficit that implies, along with a daily intake target.
how: Enter your current weight and your goal weight. Switch between lbs and kg with the toggle.
Set the target date.
Enter your maintenance calories (TDEE) if you know it.
Read the required daily deficit and the resulting daily intake.
method: The standard estimate is that a pound of body fat represents roughly 3,500 calories. Losing a set number of pounds by a set date gives a total deficit, and dividing it by the number of days gives the daily figure.

This is a planning estimate, not a physical law. Metabolic rate falls as you lose weight, water weight moves the scale by several pounds independently of fat, and the 3,500 figure is an approximation. Treat the output as a starting point to adjust from, not a prescription.

example.setup: Using the values the calculator loads with:
example.result: Spread over 12 weeks that is roughly a 625 calorie daily deficit, meaning about 1,575 calories a day.

uses: Checking whether a goal date is realistic before committing to it.
Seeing what moving the deadline out by a month does to the daily target.
Turning a vague intention into a specific daily number.
Sanity-checking a target someone else has set for you.
mistakes: Setting a deadline that requires an extreme deficit. Very large deficits are hard to sustain and cost muscle as well as fat.
Treating TDEE as fixed. It falls as you lose weight, so the same intake produces a smaller deficit over time.
Reading day-to-day scale movement as fat change. Most of it is water and food in transit.
notes: This is a general fitness estimate and not medical advice. Talk to a doctor before starting a significant calorie deficit, particularly if you have any medical condition.

daily-water-intake.intro: Daily Water Intake Calculator estimates how much water to aim for based on your body weight, activity level and climate, then lets you track what you have actually drunk through the day.
how: Enter your weight and choose lbs/oz or kg/ml units.
Pick your activity level, from sedentary through athlete.
Pick your climate: temperate, hot or humid, or cool.
Read the target and log glasses as you drink them.
method: The common starting point is roughly half your body weight in pounds, expressed in fluid ounces. At 170 pounds that is about 85 ounces before adjustments.

Activity and climate then adjust it. Exercise adds fluid loss through sweat and breathing, and hot or humid conditions add more. Cold climates reduce the requirement slightly but not as much as people expect, because cold air is dry and you still lose water breathing.

example.setup: The default profile:
example.result: A daily target in ounces, with the tracker counting what you have logged against it.

uses: Setting a concrete target instead of guessing.
Adjusting intake on training days or in hot weather.
Tracking through the day so you notice a shortfall before the evening.
Building a habit with a visible count.
mistakes: Treating the target as a hard requirement. Food contributes a meaningful share of daily fluid, and thirst is a reasonable guide for most healthy people.
Drinking a very large volume in a short time rather than spreading it out.
Counting only plain water. Tea, coffee and most drinks contribute too.
notes: This is a general guideline, not medical advice. Anyone with a kidney, heart or fluid-restriction condition should follow their doctor's guidance instead.

wind-chill.intro: Wind Chill Calculator gives the feels-like temperature in both directions: wind chill for cold conditions and heat index for hot ones. Enter the actual temperature plus wind speed or humidity and it does the rest, in Fahrenheit or Celsius.
how: Choose Wind Chill for cold weather or Heat Index for hot.
Enter the air temperature, then the wind speed for chill or the relative humidity for heat index.
Switch between Fahrenheit and Celsius as needed.
wind-chill.method_title: Two different formulas for two different problems
method: Wind chill uses the 2001 US and Canadian standard: 35.74 + 0.6215T - 35.75V^0.16 + 0.4275T x V^0.16, with T in Fahrenheit and V in miles per hour. It models how fast moving air strips the thin layer of warm air off exposed skin.

Heat index solves the opposite problem. In hot weather the danger is that high humidity stops sweat evaporating, so the body cannot shed heat. It is a function of temperature and relative humidity, and wind speed barely matters.

example.setup: A cold, windy day using the default inputs:
example.result: A wind chill of about 19 F. The air is 30 degrees, but exposed skin loses heat as if it were 19.

uses: Deciding what to wear before going out in wind.
Judging frostbite risk, which depends on wind chill rather than air temperature.
Checking whether outdoor work or exercise is safe.
Understanding why a still 20 degree day feels warmer than a windy 30 degree one.
mistakes: Applying wind chill outside its valid range. The formula is defined for temperatures at or below 50 F and wind above 3 mph.
Using wind chill for objects. It describes heat loss from exposed skin. A parked car cools to the air temperature, not to the wind chill.
Ignoring humidity in heat. At 95 F the difference between dry and humid air is the difference between uncomfortable and dangerous.

date-calculator.intro: Date Calculator does the two date jobs people actually need: how far apart two dates are, and what date falls a given distance from another. It can count weekdays only, which is what most deadlines really mean.
how: For a difference, set a start and end date and read the gap.
Switch between All days and Weekdays only depending on what you are counting.
To project forward or back, set a base date, an amount, and a unit of days, weeks, months or years.
date-calculator.method_title: Why date arithmetic is harder than it looks
method: Days and weeks are fixed lengths, so adding them is simple. Months and years are not. Adding one month to 31 January has no obvious answer, and different systems resolve it differently.

Leap years add another wrinkle. A year is 365 days except when it is 366, and the rule is that a year divisible by 4 is a leap year unless it is divisible by 100, unless it is also divisible by 400. That is why 2000 was a leap year and 1900 was not.
uses: Counting business days to a deadline, where weekends do not count.
Working out a date 90 days from now for a contract or notice period.
Finding how many days until an event.
Calculating an age or a tenure in exact days.
mistakes: Counting calendar days when the deadline means business days, or the reverse. The difference on a 30 day period is about nine days.
Forgetting whether the start day itself counts. Inclusive and exclusive counting differ by one, which matters for legal notice periods.
Assuming weekdays only means working days. It does not remove public holidays.

percentage-calculator.intro: Percentage Calculator handles the four percentage questions people actually ask, each in its own box: what is X percent of Y, X is what percent of Y, percentage change between two numbers, and adding or subtracting a percentage from a number. Every result copies with one click.
how: Pick the box that matches your question.
Enter the two numbers.
Read the answer and press Copy if you need it elsewhere.
method: Percent of: multiply the number by the percentage and divide by 100. 15 percent of 200 is 200 x 15 / 100 = 30.

Is what percent: divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100. Percentage change: subtract the old value from the new, divide by the old value, multiply by 100. Add or subtract: multiply by (100 plus or minus the percentage) divided by 100.

example.setup: The default values, showing the first two calculations are inverses of each other:
example.result: The same relationship read in both directions, which is the check most percentage errors fail.

uses: Working out a discount or a tax amount.
Calculating percentage growth between two figures.
Adding a markup or taking off a discount.
Checking a figure someone else has quoted.
mistakes: Assuming a percentage increase and decrease cancel out. Add 10% then subtract 10% and you land at 99% of where you started, not 100%.
Confusing percentage points with percent. Going from 5% to 7% is a rise of 2 percentage points but a 40% increase.
Using the wrong base for percentage change. The change is always measured against the original value.

temperature-converter.intro: Temperature Converter moves between Fahrenheit, Celsius and Kelvin. Type into any of the three fields and the other two follow.
how: Type a value into whichever scale you have.
Read the other two scales immediately.
method: Celsius to Fahrenheit multiplies by 9/5 and adds 32. Fahrenheit to Celsius subtracts 32 first, then multiplies by 5/9. The subtraction has to come first because the two scales have different zero points as well as different degree sizes.
Kelvin is Celsius shifted so that zero is absolute zero, the point where molecular motion stops. Kelvin equals Celsius plus 273.15, and there are no negative Kelvin values.

example.setup: Three temperatures worth knowing:
example.result: Minus 40 is the one temperature where Celsius and Fahrenheit give the same number.

uses: Converting a recipe oven temperature between conventions.
Reading a weather forecast from another country.
Converting scientific data, which is usually in Celsius or Kelvin.
Checking a fever reading against a scale you are unfamiliar with.
mistakes: Multiplying before subtracting when going from Fahrenheit to Celsius. The 32 must come off first.
Writing degrees Kelvin. Kelvin has no degree symbol, it is just kelvin.
Converting a temperature difference the same way as a temperature. A change of 10 C is a change of 18 F, with no offset applied.

net-worth-tracker.intro: Net Worth Tracker adds up what you own and subtracts what you owe. Enter assets and liabilities with your own labels and it keeps a running total, entirely in your browser.
how: Add each asset with a name and a value.
Add each liability the same way.
Read the net worth figure, which updates as you go.
method: Net worth is assets minus liabilities. Assets are things you own that have value: cash, savings, investments, retirement accounts, property, vehicles. Liabilities are what you owe: mortgage, car loans, student loans, credit card balances.

A house belongs on both sides. The property's market value is an asset and the outstanding mortgage is a liability. Listing only one of the two is the most common way people get a wildly wrong figure.
uses: Getting a single number for your financial position rather than a scatter of account balances.
Tracking progress over time, which matters more than any single snapshot.
Seeing the effect of paying down debt versus saving.
Preparing figures before a mortgage or loan application.
mistakes: Valuing assets optimistically. Use what something would actually sell for, not what you paid or hope to get.
Forgetting depreciating assets. A car loses value every year and the loan does not shrink as fast.
Panicking at a negative number. Early in a career, with student debt and no equity, negative net worth is normal and temporary.
notes: Everything stays in your browser. No account, no upload, and nothing is transmitted anywhere.

haiku-checker.intro: Haiku Checker counts syllables line by line and tells you whether your poem matches the 5-7-5 pattern. Type each line into its own field and the counts update as you write.
how: Type the first line and watch the syllable count.
Fill in the second and third lines.
Adjust wording until the counts read 5, 7 and 5.
haiku-checker.method_title: How syllables are counted, and why it is imperfect
method: Syllable counting works by finding vowel groups in a word, then correcting for the common English exceptions: a silent final e, the -le ending that adds a syllable, and vowel pairs that form one sound rather than two.

English defeats any purely mechanical rule. Fire and flower are one or two syllables depending on your accent, and words like every are routinely compressed in speech. Treat the count as a strong guide and trust your ear where they disagree.

example.setup: The classic structure:
example.result: Seventeen syllables total, the English convention adapted from the Japanese form.

uses: Writing haiku without counting on your fingers.
Teaching syllables and meter in a classroom.
Checking a line quickly while drafting other poetry.
Tightening prose, since syllable count is a decent proxy for how heavy a sentence reads.
mistakes: Treating 5-7-5 as the definition of haiku. Traditional Japanese haiku counts on, which are not the same as English syllables, and many respected English haiku deliberately do not use 5-7-5.
Trusting the counter over your own ear on ambiguous words like fire, hour and every.

anagram-solver.intro: Anagram Solver finds words that can be made from the letters you give it, with filtering by length, and a separate checker that tells you whether two words or phrases are anagrams of each other.
how: Enter a word or phrase to find anagrams from its letters.
Filter the results by word length.
Use the second box to check whether two specific words or phrases are anagrams.
method: Two strings are anagrams if they contain exactly the same letters with the same counts. The reliable test is to strip spaces and punctuation, lowercase everything, sort the letters, and compare the results. Listen and silent both sort to eilnst.
Counting letter frequency is the faster equivalent and is what most implementations use, because it avoids sorting and handles long phrases better.

example.setup: Checking a classic pair:
example.result: Identical letter multisets, so they are anagrams.

uses: Solving crossword and puzzle clues.
Finding words in word games from a rack of letters.
Checking a supposed anagram someone has claimed.
Generating name or title ideas from a fixed set of letters.
mistakes: Forgetting that anagram checking ignores spaces and punctuation but not letter counts. Two words with the same letters in different quantities are not anagrams.
Expecting every letter combination to be a real word. The solver is limited to a dictionary, which is what makes the results useful.

leet-speak.intro: Leet Speak Translator converts text into 1337 at three intensity levels, and converts it back the other way. A character map shows exactly what each substitution is at the highest level.
how: Type or paste English text.
Set the leet level from 1 to 3. Level 1 is light, level 3 substitutes the most characters.
Read the output, or paste leet in to translate back to English.
Try one of the preset phrases if you want to see it working.
method: Leet substitutes visually similar characters for letters: 3 for E, 4 or @ for A, 1 for L or I, 0 for O, 7 for T, 5 for S. It grew out of 1980s bulletin board culture, partly as an in-group marker and partly to get around naive text filters.

The levels here control how aggressive the substitution is. Light leet stays readable at a glance. Heavy leet replaces almost every letter it can, which is why translating back is a genuinely useful feature.

example.setup: A phrase at heavy substitution:
given: E to 3, L to 1, I to 1, A to 4, C to <
example.result: Recognisably the same phrase, once your eye adjusts to reading digits as letters.

uses: Making a username when the one you want is taken.
Retro or gaming-themed graphics and titles.
Decoding leet you have run into and cannot read.
Showing kids why substitution ciphers are easy to break.
mistakes: Using leet in a password and thinking it adds security. Password crackers have applied leet substitutions as standard for decades, so P4ssw0rd is barely stronger than password.
Assuming the translation back is exact. Several letters map to the same character, so some ambiguity is unavoidable.

unicode-normalizer.intro: Unicode Normalizer converts text to any of the four standard Unicode normalization forms: NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD. It is the tool you need when two strings look identical but refuse to compare as equal.
how: Paste the text you want to normalize.
Choose a form: NFC, NFD, NFKC or NFKD.
Copy the result, or clear and start again.
method: Unicode can represent the same character in more than one way. The letter e-acute can be a single code point (U+00E9) or a plain e followed by a combining accent (U+0065 U+0301). They look identical and are not equal as strings. NFC composes them into the single code point, NFD decomposes them into the pair.

The K forms apply compatibility mapping as well, which folds visually distinct variants into plain equivalents. NFKC turns a full-width character into its ASCII equivalent and the ligature fi into f plus i. That is powerful for search and matching, and lossy, so it is the wrong choice if you need to preserve the original exactly.

example.setup: Two ways of writing the same accented letter:
given: two code points, e + combining acute
example.result: Identical on screen, unequal as strings, until you normalize both to the same form.

uses: Fixing a string comparison that fails even though both values look the same.
Cleaning text pasted from macOS, which often uses decomposed forms, before storing it.
Normalizing user input before saving usernames or search keys.
Debugging why a database lookup misses on an accented name.
mistakes: Using NFKC when you need to preserve the original text. Compatibility mapping discards distinctions you may need later.
Normalizing only one side of a comparison. Both strings must be in the same form for the comparison to be meaningful.
Assuming ASCII text is unaffected. It is not changed, which is precisely why normalizing everything on input is safe and cheap.

color-temperature.intro: Color Temperature Converter turns a Kelvin value into an RGB hex colour and shows the swatch, across the full range from 1000 K to 12000 K. It includes reference points for the light sources you actually encounter.
how: Drag the slider or type a Kelvin value between 1000 and 12000.
Read the hex colour and see the swatch update.
Compare against the reference points for common light sources.
method: Colour temperature describes the colour of light emitted by an idealised black body heated to that temperature. Low temperatures glow red and orange. As the temperature rises the light shifts through white and into blue.

This runs directly against everyday language, where red is a warm colour and blue is a cool one. A 2700 K bulb is called warm white and a 6500 K bulb is called cool daylight, even though 6500 K is physically much hotter. The names follow how the light feels, not the physics.

example.setup: Common sources across the range:
example.result: The default 6500 K sits at daylight, which is why it is the standard white point for monitors.

uses: Matching a light source when setting white balance for photo or video.
Choosing bulbs that match each other across a room.
Picking a screen colour temperature for editing or for evening reading.
Reproducing a specific lighting mood in a design.
mistakes: Reading higher Kelvin as warmer. It is the opposite, and the naming convention makes this a persistent trap.
Mixing colour temperatures in one room. Two bulbs 2000 K apart will look obviously wrong together even though each looks fine alone.
Setting camera white balance to daylight indoors, which gives everything an orange cast from tungsten lighting.

qr-code-generator.intro: QR Code Generator makes a downloadable QR code from a URL, plain text, WiFi credentials, an email address, a phone number, an SMS or a contact card. Size, colours, margin and error correction are all adjustable, and the result downloads as a PNG.
how: Pick a preset (URL, WiFi, Email, Phone, SMS, Contact) or type your content directly.
Set the size between 64 and 1024 pixels.
Choose an error correction level and adjust the colours and margin.
Download the PNG.
qr-code-generator.method_title: What error correction actually buys you
method: QR codes carry redundant data so they still scan when part of the code is damaged, dirty or covered. The four levels recover roughly 7, 15, 25 and 30 percent of the code: Low, Medium, Quartile and High.

Higher correction is not free. The redundancy takes space, so the same content at High produces a denser code than at Low. Use Medium for anything on a screen, and Quartile or High for print, for stickers that will get scuffed, or when you plan to place a logo over the centre.

example.setup: Choosing a level for a printed sign:
example.result: A code that still scans with a quarter of it obscured, at the cost of a denser pattern than Low would give.

uses: Putting a link on a printed poster, menu or business card.
Sharing WiFi credentials with guests without reading out the password.
Adding a contact card to printed material.
Linking a physical product to instructions or a registration page.
mistakes: Printing too small. Below about two centimetres most phone cameras struggle, especially with a dense code.
Removing the quiet zone. The blank margin around a QR code is part of the specification and scanners need it.
Inverting the colours. Most scanners expect a dark code on a light background, and a light-on-dark code fails on many readers.
Choosing low contrast. Pale colours look nicer and scan far worse.
